# Could power supply in northern Chile transmit higher copper prices? In 2011, arid northern Chile accounted for 20% of global mined copper production. This area is served by the _Sistema Interconectado del Norte Grande_ (SING) electric grid. The copper industry accounts for about 90% of demand in the SING but new copper mines will have higher power requirements than existing mines due to their need to use desalinated seawater. If northern Chile does not increase its power supply, copper production could falter. It is forecast that current generation and LNG import capacities are sufficient to support the growth plans of copper miners in northern Chile until 2018. Beyond this date, northern Chile will need access to more generation capacity if mine development is not to be impeded by unreliable power supply. Since increasing energy imports from neighbouring countries is unlikely, the problem of power supply in northern Chile must be solved within the country. Although connecting the SING with the _Sistema Interconectado Central_ (SIC) network that serves the central part of the country would be a partial solution, additional generating capacity will still be required. However, building new power capacity anywhere in Chile has proven difficult due to environmental regulations. If Chile does not increase power supply, copper production in the north could be constrained and would contribute to a tight global market for mined copper over the next 20 years – and may impact global copper prices. Could power supply in northern Chile transmit higher copper prices? ## Chilean power supply is important to copper Chile’s mined copper production during 2011 was 5.29 Mt (33% of the global total). Of this amount 3.33 Mt (63%) was produced at mines in the northernmost part of the country. Power demand is forecast to increase in northern Chile. This is due to the development of new copper mining projects, falling head grades which mean that more ore must be treated to produce the same amount of copper and the future requirement to use desalinated water at minesites. Since Chile has few domestic energy resources and cannot rely on its neighbours, an opportunity exists to develop import terminals, generation capacity and transmission lines. #### **Map of Chile showing area covered by SING and SIC electricity networks** 72°W 70°W 68°W 66°W Chile has two major power grids. Chile has two major power grids. The _Sistema Interconectado Central_ (SIC) network serves the central part of the country, home to over 90% of Chile’s population, while the _Sistema Interconectado del Norte Grande_ (SING) grid supplies the northern part of the country. While power demand in the SIC is dominated by small end users (i.e. households), 90% of power demand in the SING is from mining and other large industrial consumers. The area covered by the SING contains the world’s most arid desert and copper mines will need to desalin

ate and pump water for their operations. Desalination and pumping water are very power intensive and the SING will need to develop additional generation capacity. In 2005, the SING generated over 60% of its electricity fromArgentine gas. However from 2006 Argentina began to Argentine gas. However from 2006 Argentina began to reduce gas exports to Chile. This left Chile, particularly the north, scrambling for new gas and energy supplies. This led to a surge in the use of expensive oil products until theMejillones LNG regas terminal came online in 2010. While Mejillones LNG regas terminal came online in 2010. While Argentina has the gas resources to supply Chile, poor Argentine regulation means that Chile will be unable to rely on it for gas. Apart from some hydro potential and a coal mine in the south, Chile does not have any substantial energy resources. This makes Chile, especially the north, dependent on energy imports. While Chile’s neighbours (Peru, Bolivia, Argentina) could export gas to Chile, politics means that Chile cannot rely on these markets. In short, power demand is going to increase and since Chile cannot rely on its neighbours it must develop power capacity which is fuelled by energy imported from further afield. If Chile is unable to increase power supply, copper production could be constrained and the impact on prices would be global. Metals Cost Service Insight - September 2012 Page 2 of 8 Could power supply in northern Chile transmit higher copper prices? ## Power costs to Chilean copper mines Average power costs paid by copper mines in Chile during 2010 were 12c/kWh, the highest for any major copper producing country and 50% higher than the global average of 8c/kWh. Electricity represented 16% of minesite costs at Chilean mines compared to 12% globally making up a smaller component of minesite costs than other inputs such as consumables and labour. During 2010, average C1 cash operating costs in Chile were 112c/lb (compared to 104c/lb globally). With the copper price averaging 340c/lb during that year it can be argued that high electricity prices only had a marginal impact on the operating profits enjoyed by Chilean copper miners. However, in future years as the industry experiences rapid cost escalation on all inputs and the copper price trends towards a long term average, forecast to be in the region of 300c/lb cash operating margins will become more squeezed. Stable electricity prices will become an important requirement for those companies seeking to develop and operate copper mines in the northern part of Chile. #### **C1 cash operating cost structure for major copper producing countries (2010)** By Product Credit Delta

## Copper mine production trends in SING area It is estimated that about 14,200 GWh of electrical energy was delivered to end-users on the SING during 2011, of this about 11,900 GWh was directly consumed by copper mines with a further 750 GWh consumed by copper smelters and related industries. Overall consumption attributable to the copper industry was about 12,700GWh (90% of the total delivered electricity). Over the next decade and beyond the power requirements of the regions copper mines will be influenced by several production trends. ### **Falling head grades mean that more ore must be processed to produce the same amount of copper** Copper mines in northern Chile are facing a long term trend of declining head grades due to higher grade ore at existing mines being depleted. Higher metal prices also enable lower grade material to be categorised as commercially exploitable ore. This trend means that more ore needs to be treated to produce the same amount of copper with consequentially higher power requirements. ### **Using desalinated seawater requires more electricity** A typical milling operation in northern Chile, using water from local aquifers, consumes around 23 kWh/t of ore milled. However, due to the scarcity of water in the area it is highly probable that any new mine development including brownfield expansions will be required to use seawater. Since most mines are located at elevations of 3000m above sea level (a.s.l.) or higher the additional electrical power requirements to pump seawater to the mine sites are considerable. For a typical mine located 3500m a.s.l. and 180 km from the coast that consumes 0.5 m3 of water for every tonne of ore treated, it is estimated that the requirement to pump seawater would add 9 kWh/t of ore treated to the power requirements of the mine. Although some plants, notably Antofagasta Minerals Esperanza operation, utilise untreated seawater it is probable that most seawater used at copper mines in the future will go through a desalination process. Desalination reduces additional plant maintenance requirements caused by the corrosive nature of seawater and also Metals Cost Service Insight - September 2012 Page 3 of 8 Could power supply in northern Chile transmit higher copper prices? mitigates any negative impact that using untreated seawater may have on recovery of copper in the flotation process. If an average power requirement of 4 kWh/m3 of water is assumed for a reverse osmosis plant, then the requirement to use desalinated water adds a further 2 kWh/t of ore treated. For a typical mine the requirement to use desalinated seawater therefore increases the power required from 23 kWh/t of ore to 34 kWh/t. Although the existing Michilla SxEw operation uses seawater as the Cl- content is beneficial to their leaching process, it is assumed that generally as SxEw operations consume less water tha

n mills they will not be required to switch to seawater. 

### **Decline in SxEw production** 

Copper mine production is by two main process routes.  The first of these is the leaching of oxide ores with sulphuric acid followed by the recovery of copper cathode from the resulting pregnant leach solution by the solvent extraction and electro-winning (SxEw) process.  The second route is the production of copper in concentrate from the processing of sulphide ores in a milling and flotation plan.  Of the 3.33Mt of copper mine production in the SING region in 2011, 1.79Mt (54%) was produced via the SxEw route, this compares with a figure of 38% for Chile as a whole.  Most copper orebodies in the north of Chile are classic porphyry copper deposits whereby primary sulphide mineralisation underlies a layer of oxidised ore.  Consequently oxidised reserves, which are generally mined earlier in the life of a mine are expected to become depleted over the coming years.  By 2025 it is forecast that mined copper production from base case mines and probable projects in the SING grid area will be 2.87Mt of which 626kt (22%) will be from SxEw.  On average SxEw producers on northern Chile consumed around 3,500 kWh/tonne of copper produced during 2011.  This is around 10% higher than the comparable figure for copper in concentrate producers, so if all other factors remained equal this shift from SxEw cathode production to copper in concentrate production would free up some electrical generating capacity for additional milling base mine expansions.  Although this trend only partially mitigates the increased power requirements brought about by falling head grades and the requirement for mines to use seawater. 

### **Brownfield projects are a crucial source of incremental copper production capacity** 

For the reasons described above, brownfield developments represent the natural evolution of northern Chile’s copper mining sector.  These will comprise the construction of milling and flotation plants at mines where production is currently via the SxEw process and the expansion of existing milling facilities in order to realise the economies of scale necessary to economically exploit lower grade ores.  Brownfield projects are also attractive to mining companies as some or all of the infrastructure required will already be in place, thereby reducing capital investment requirements compared to an equivalent greenfield development. Additionally, since the orebody is already being mined its technical characteristics will be to some extent understood reducing technical risk involved. 

Base case copper mine production in the SING region, which includes operating mines and those projects which are currently in construction is due to decline from around 2015 as reserves become depleted (low case).  Projects, which are currently sufficiently advanced to be regarded as ‘probable; have the potential to maintain production in the region at around 4Mt/a until around the end of thi

s decade, before gradually declining (mid scenario). ## Will there be enough electricity? 28,127 GWh of electricity can be generated in the SING with its current generation and LNG import capacities. In the high scenario, power demand will exceed this in 2019. However, even in the low and medium scenarios, the fleet capacity factor is worryingly high. After adjusting for LNG import capacity, in 2019 the fleet capacity factor will average 81% in the medium case and 65% in the low case. This margin is not sufficient for reliable power supply because all grids experience unexpected surges in power demand and unplanned power plant outages. By comparison, the United States average power plant utilisation is about 45%. #### **SING power generation by fuel and SING Demand forecas

Development of all ‘probable’ projects in the SING would increase total electrical demand to 23,000 GWh by 2017 and if all the ‘possible’ mining projects currently under consideration were developed then the total power demand would exceed 39,000 GWh by 2025. In all scenarios, power consumed by the non-mining sectors will increase from almost 4,000 GWh in 2011 to almost 7,400 GWh in 2025. If existing milling operations were required to switch to desalinated water then additional annual power requirements due to this would peak at 3,400 GWh over the period 2016 to 2020. Note that SING demand scenarios in the chart above do not assume that existing milling operations will have to desalinate and pump water. Furthermore, many existing power plants also require water and if mining operations struggle with freshwater supply, power plants may also struggle. ## How can Chile fix this power problem? To ensure reliable power, the SING has four options. Firstly it can add additional generation capacity and expand LNG import capacity. Secondly, if the SING and SIC grids were connected, it would essentially increase the SING’s access to electricity. Thirdly, the SING could increase/start importing electricity from its neighbours. Finally if demand was reduced there would be sufficient generation capacity. Each of these options has their own advantages but ultimately the long term solution is to build new generation capacity in the SING and connect the SING and SIC. ### **Increase Generation Capacity** In theory, increasing generation capacity is the most effective, cheapest and most feasible option available to the SING. By increasing generation capacity the SING can lower capacity utilisation which will decrease the likelihood of unplanned power outages. Depending on which type of capacity is added, power prices may also decrease. However, there are no major power plants under construction in the SING and there are concerns about the ability to develop power generation capacity anywhere in Chile. The Chilean government has reject several major power projects despite having approval from the relevant regulatory authorities. Particularly w

orrying was the Supreme Court’s ruling in late August 2012 that the 2.1 GW coal-fired Castilla power plant violated the constitution on environmental grounds. Castilla had been issued environmental permits in February 2011. Environmental concerns extend to hydro power as shown in the difficulties in developing the 2.75 GW HidroAysen dam in the south. Despite these setbacks, it is likely that Chile will still develop additional hydro and coal fired generation capacity. #### **High-level advantages and disadvantages of different types of power generation** |**Fuel**|**Advantages**|**Disadvantages**|**Comment**| |---|---|---|---| |Coal|Cheap and established energy source.

### **Connect the SING and SIC grids** 

Chile has two separate power grids, which if connected would increase reliability and power supply to the SING. Furthermore by connecting the grids, the SING would gain access to relatively cheap hydro in the SIC.  Several new hydro dams are planned for the SIC including the controversial 2.75 GW HidroAysйn dam.  However, connecting the two grids would be expensive with estimates ranging between US$ 500 million to US$ 1 billion. 

The SIC is substantially larger than the northern grid SING with an installed capacity of 12.1 GW compared to 3.7 GW in the SING.  Furthermore, gross generation in the SIC is almost three times larger than the SING.  About 90% of delivered power demand in the SING is by the copper industry, while 70% of power demand in the SIC, is from small end-users (i.e. households).  Daily and yearly demand vary between the two grids, therefore by connecting the SIC and SING, variations in power demand can be met with generation from a different part of the country.  Also hydro generation supplies between 45-70% of electricity to the SIC and when drought occurs it could pull electricity from the SING. 

In August 2012, there were reports that the Chilean government would tender a SING-SIC interconnection in H1 2013. The transmission line would be 610 km and would cost about US$ 700 million.  While it is likely that the two grids will be eventually connected, the long distance power transmission would result in higher losses. 

### **Reduce demand** 

By reducing demand in the SING, the existing power capacity would be sufficient to meet future demands.  Since the mining sector accounts for 90% of delivered demand in the SING, new less-power intensive copper production techniques will need to develop.  As power demand becomes increasingly driven by desalination and pumping, then those technologies will need a technological breakthrough to substantially lower demand.  The use of High Pressure Grinding Rolls (HPGR) instead of the standard SAG mills is one potential way that the power consumed by copper mines can be significantly reduced.  Although this technology has been successfully implemented at the Cerro Verde mine in neighbouring Peru, it is yet to be shown whether it can be effective on Chilean ores. 

The energy intensity of desalination and pumping is not unique to northern Chile.  Global concerns over water security, particularly in the Middle East, has led to substantial investment in desalination technology.  While there is potential to reduce power used in pumping and desalination, it is unlikely that any improvements would be sufficient to substantially reduce electricity demand growth. 

### **Import Electricity from its Neighbours** 

Chile could meet its future power needs by importing electricity from its neighbours.  However, diplomatic relations between Chile

and its neighbours are poor.  Transmission lines currently link northern Chile with a 643 MW power plant in Salta, Argentina.  Peru and Bolivia grids are not linked to Chile. 

The 643 MW power plant in Argentina capable of exporting power to Chile is owned by AES Gener and was partially developed for the Chile market.  However, Argentina is experiencing energy shortages and power exports to Chile have decreased making it unlikely Chile will want to rely on Argentina.  Furthermore, Argentina has proven unreliable for gas supplies and since security of supply is important to Chile, Argentina will not be a viable long term option for electricity. 

The War of the Pacific (1879-1904) pitted Chile against Peru and Bolivia.  The result of the war gave Chile much of its northern territory and made Bolivia a landlocked nation.  Diplomatic relations between Chile, Peru and Bolivia have been strained as a result.  Bolivia and Peru gas export contracts prohibit gas being sent to Chile.  Peru exports LNG and Bolivia exports gas via pipelines to Brazil and Argentina.  The gas export contract between Argentina and Bolivia states that Bolivian gas may not be sent to Chile via Argentina.  Even if Chile had better diplomatic relations with Peru and Bolivia, new transmission lines and power capacity would need to be built.  Bolivia and to a lesser extent Peru, struggle to meet their own power needs and it would be politically difficult to justify sending electricity to Chile, even if diplomatic relations improved.

## Conclusion 

Chilean miners face the highest power costs of any major copper producing country.  Although these levels are not currently prohibitive to the profitable operation of mining operations, as the production of copper in the northern part of the country becomes more power intensive, securing a reliable power supply at a reasonable tariff will become increasingly critical to the region’s attractiveness as a location for developing copper mining projects. 

Chile is to copper what Saudi Arabia is to oil, therefore power supply issues in the country will have repercussions to the global mine supply of the metal.  Electricity demand in the north will increase as mines need to desalinate seawater and pump it to high altitude mines.  Furthermore, falling ore grades will require more water and electricity to process. 

However, the northern grid is isolated and relatively small.  Since developing new power capacity in Chile is difficult due to environmental regulation, power supply could start to affect copper production as soon as 2018. 

If power supply is not available it will restrain mining development in Chile.  With increased power imports from neighbouring countries unlikely, the most viable option would be to add more generating capacity and connect the SING and SIC grids.  While new ge

neration capacity has recently struggled to get the relevant environmental permits, new capacity will be added.  This is because the impact on copper production and the economy from power shortages would be so severe that politicians will be forced to act.  Furthermore, the Chilean government has experience dealing with more severe energy crises as demonstrated by how it managed to avoid major power outages after Argentina ceased gas exports in 2007. 

Our view is that Chile will avoid a major power crisis.  However, it is likely that power supply will become an important issue in increasing copper production.  This would contribute to a tight global market for mined copper and could increase prices.  So Chile could also become another example of how a local problem can have global repercussions.
